Seminar Title:

Investigating the Impact of Political Marketing on Electoral Patronage Behaviour

Seminar Type:

Progress Seminar

Department:

Speaker Type:

Student

Arvind Kumar

Abstract:

Contemporary electoral democracies are undergoing profound transformations driven by rapid digitalisation, expanding political information environments, and increasing electoral competition. Political parties increasingly utilise digital political communication, data-driven campaign strategies, political branding, and leadership positioning to shape voter perceptions and cultivate long-term electoral support. Simultaneously, the rise of digitally coordinated Generation Z-led political mobilisation in India has highlighted the growing influence of young citizens in shaping public discourse, demanding political accountability, and influencing governance through social media-enabled participation. These developments underscore the importance of the credibility of political information, governance performance, political branding, and trust in understanding contemporary electoral behaviour. Despite growing interest in political marketing and voting behaviour, existing studies have largely examined political branding, digital political communication, governance performance, welfare policy perception, and political trust independently, with limited attention to their combined influence on long-term Electoral Patronage Behaviour, particularly among Generation Z voters in emerging democracies. Addressing this gap, the present study proposes an integrated conceptual framework to examine how digital political communication, information credibility, data-driven campaign strategies, welfare policy perception, governance performance, political brand personality, and perceived leadership credibility influence Political Brand Image, Political Brand Trust, Political Brand Preference, and ultimately Electoral Patronage Behaviour among Generation Z voters in Bihar, Jharkhand, and West Bengal. The study is grounded in the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), Signalling Theory, Social Identity Theory, Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB), and the Customer-Based Brand Equity (CBBE) framework. A sequential mixed-method design is adopted, combining qualitative exploration through semi-structured interviews with a subsequent quantitative survey analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The study is expected to advance the political marketing literature by developing and empirically validating an integrated framework that explains long-term Electoral Patronage Behaviour among Generation Z voters, while providing practical insights for political parties and policymakers to strengthen political communication, build public trust, and enhance democratic engagement.
